programme: KLF10 and KLF14 — paralogous Kruppel-like, TGF-beta-responsive zinc-finger factors — both target the core TGF-beta/SMAD module (KLF10: SMAD2, SMAD3, SMAD4, SMAD7, TGFB1; KLF14: TGFBR2) and both target FOXP3, the lineage-defining transcription factor of regulatory T cells. Together they sit upstream of TGF-beta-driven induction of FOXP3+ regulatory T cells, i.e. a Treg-differentiation/immunosuppression programme, not a generic TGF-beta fibrosis programme.
role_in_a: Not documented in the retrieved record for fibromyalgia. If this axis is active in blood, the expected effect is on circulating Treg frequency/suppressive tone rather than a classical autoimmune signature — consistent with the low-grade immune dysregulation proposed in fibromyalgia's wider literature, but that connection is inferred, not evidenced here.
role_in_b: In head and neck carcinoma, TGF-beta-driven FOXP3+ Treg infiltration is a documented immunosuppressive mechanism in the tumor microenvironment: FOXP3 is used for immune-cell quantification and prognosis, is radiomics-predictable, and is now a direct therapeutic target (an antisense oligonucleotide against FOXP3 mRNA). The retrieved evidence sits on FOXP3 itself, the shared downstream node of KLF10 and KLF14, not on the two factors directly.
shared_axis: Both diseases could converge on the same lever — TGF-beta/SMAD signalling setting local FOXP3+ Treg tone — with opposite clinical stakes: suppressing anti-tumor immunity in the head-and-neck tumor bed versus shaping systemic immune/inflammatory tone in fibromyalgia blood. Nothing in the retrieved record states this connection for fibromyalgia; it is a mechanistic hypothesis built by tracing KLF10/KLF14's shared target, not a documented finding.
reasoning: The programme is nameable and textbook-coherent (KLF10/KLF14 -> SMAD/TGFB1/TGFBR2 -> FOXP3 -> Treg induction), and FOXP3 itself is well placed in HNC by four papers. But FOXP3 is marked discordant here and so is not a carrying factor, and neither KLF10 nor KLF14 has any Open Targets association or on-topic paper in either disease (KLF10's only hit is endometriosis) — the retrieved record never reaches the carrying factors themselves, and rheumatology/pain and head-and-neck oncology have no obvious anatomical or clinical overlap to justify the link independently.
support: PMID 39937271 — AZD8701, an antisense oligonucleotide against FOXP3 mRNA, tested in head and neck cancer, showing FOXP3-driven Treg activity is directly druggable in this tumor; PMID 38376584 — radiomics features predict FOXP3 expression and clinical prognosis in head and neck cancer, placing FOXP3 as a clinically tracked immune node; PMID 39826685 — deep-learning immune cell quantification in radiotherapy-treated head and neck cancer, part of the same FOXP3/Treg immune-profiling literature; PMID 36900270 — tumor microenvironment and immune response in lip cancer, a head-and-neck subtype context for FOXP3-marked Tregs. None of these mention KLF10 or KLF14 directly, and no paper places this axis in fibromyalgia.
how_to_falsify: In PBMCs from fibromyalgia patients versus matched controls, measure KLF10/KLF14 expression alongside TGF-beta target genes (SMAD7, SERPINE1) and FOXP3+ Treg frequency/suppressive capacity; no shift relative to controls would falsify a fibromyalgia role for this axis. In HNC tumor tissue or cell lines, knock down KLF10 and KLF14 and test whether FOXP3 induction and Treg differentiation from co-cultured naive T cells drop; if FOXP3 induction is unchanged, KLF10/KLF14 are not the drivers of the documented FOXP3/Treg signal in this tumor.
caveats: Tissue pairing is blood (fibromyalgia) versus head-and-neck tissue (HNC), so 'agreement' here means concordant target-gene direction across many independently-fit patient-group networks, not activity in the same cell type or site — and only 1 independent cohort pair underlies the 184 patient-group comparisons, so replication is thin despite the large comparison count. FOXP3, the node that actually carries the retrieved evidence, is explicitly discordant and therefore excluded from the carrying factors — its literature support does not itself demonstrate shared regulation across the two diseases. The tissue-generic exclusion list removes several other T-cell/lymphocyte regulators (FOXO1, LEF1, TCF7, BCL6, NFATC2, SPIB), so this account is not simply restating a routine tissue-generic T-cell signature; but with the carrying factors themselves unplaced in Open Targets or the literature, and several other concordant factors (IRF9's interferon-stimulated-gene set, MEF2A/MYF6 muscle-programme targets, BCLAF1, NUPR1, SIRT6, ZNF410, NFX1) not folding into this or any other single coherent story, the account should be read as one plausible thread among an otherwise unexplained factor list, not as the dominant relationship between these two diseases.
